content.confidence: 3: You are fairly confident in your assessment. It is possible that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work. Math/other details were not carefully checked.
content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes a two-stage framework to improve adversarial robustness of NLP systems. Firstly, a randomized smoothing (RS) strategy is adapted for discrete text inputs. Then, a  gradient-guided masked inference (MI) approach is used to reinforce the smoothing effect of RS. The framework is applied in large-scale pre-trained language models. Experimental results on three benchmark datasets show that the proposed framework achieves obtains improvements of robustness compared with existing methods. Overall, the key idea is to mask the salient tokens in the input instead of random selections used in the standard masked language modeling.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength: 

1. A simple gradient-based adversarial training framework is proposed. The framework is applicable to various pre-trained language models.

2. The results show non-trivial improvements in adversarial robustness.

Weaknesses:

1. The results are not fully comparable with existing studies. "We build development sets for IMDB, AG, and QNLI by randomly drawing 10% samples from each training set via a stratified sampling strategy." It is reasonable to use a small set for evaluations due to the slow running speed of attacking methods. However, there are two possible concerns. 

Firstly, the results may vary in each sampling. Is there any cross-validation experiment to show the results are convincing? Besides, the results may also be hard to reproduce. 

Secondly, the numbers (e.g., in Table 2) are thus not comparable with the original baselines. For example, in the FreeLM paper, the BERT and FreeLB results are 90.5/91.8 for QNLI. However, in this paper, the BERT and FreeLB results are 79.5/85.6, which are much lower than the original ones. Similar cases also happen in the IMDB dataset. It will be easier to justify whether the proposed method benefits SAcc if the author can report the SAccs on the entire test sets. As an alternative, why not choose small datasets such as RTE?

2. A key ablation study of the effect of masking is missing. The effectiveness seems to depend on the special mask token (e.g., [MASK] in BERT).  

1) The proposed method can be regarded as an MLM-like objective. A more fair baseline for comparison is using random masking, e.g., masking salient tokens with random tokens instead of perturbations generated by an attack algorithm.

2) The method may be only applicable to BERT-style language models. How about the results when using other tokens   (e.g., [PAD], [UNK]) without specific meanings? 

3. It is not clear how the framework improves robustness. It is pleased that the proposed method achieves non-trivial results on RAcc and ASR. The source of gain is still not clear. 

For example, what is the divergence of the output embeddings of the encoder? And what about the attention matrix is like?

The common point of RSMI and text attack (e.g., TextFooler, BAE) are that they both pick out the Top-K important tokens and replace them. It may help if the author demonstrates which tokens in the sentence are more likely to be chosen guided by the gradient.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: This paper is well-written, and most parts are well-clarified. The method is novel to some extent. The experimental part may not be quite reproducible.

content.title: Response to Reviewer epeZ (Part 1).
content.comment:
### The results are not fully comparable with existing studies. "We build development sets for IMDB, AG, and QNLI by randomly drawing 10% samples from each training set via a stratified sampling strategy." It is reasonable to use a small set for evaluations due to the slow running speed of attacking methods. However, there are two possible concerns.

### Firstly, the results may vary in each sampling. Is there any cross-validation experiment to show the results are convincing? Besides, the results may also be hard to reproduce.

Actually, the original test dataset size is smaller than our dev set size. The QNLI test set size is around 5k and our sampled dev set size is around 10k.  Also, we emphasized that InfoBERT and FreeLB are slower than RSMI during a training phase as shown in Table 7.  I think this answer can address your concern. Moreover. it is common practice to build a dev set for a model selection by drawing 10% samples of training sets. In addition, we already train models three times with three different random initializations.

We trained baseline algorithms three times as mentioned in the paper and the table below summarized statistics of SAcc and RAcc of each method. As shown in the table, RSMI shows significantly better stability in terms of RAcc. The instability of FreeLB and InfoBERT might be explained by their aggressive gradient update steps and contrastive learning loss [1] which is known for its sensitivity to various parameter settings. Moreover, we already uploaded the code for RSMI, you can try it if you have doubts about the reproducibility.

content.title: Response to Reviewer epeZ (Part 3.)
content.comment:
### Secondly, the numbers (e.g., in Table 2) are thus not comparable with the original baselines. For example, in the FreeLM paper, the BERT and FreeLB results are 90.5/91.8 for QNLI. However, in this paper, the BERT and FreeLB results are 79.5/85.6, which are much lower than the original ones. Similar cases also happen in the IMDB dataset. It will be easier to justify whether the proposed method benefits SAcc if the author can report the SAccs on the entire test sets. As an alternative, why not choose small datasets such as RTE?

We present the SAcc on the whole test sets. For the BERT models for QNLI cases, we found that models with early stopping tend to show better RAcc than models selected by the dev set, so we reported FreeLB and InfoBERT models with higher RAcc. Also, InfoBERT and FreeLB tend to show high fluctuations in terms of RAcc as shown in the table above.    

### A key ablation study of the effect of masking is missing. The effectiveness seems to depend on the special mask token (e.g., [MASK] in BERT) and the method may be only applicable to BERT-style language models. How about the results when using other tokens (e.g., [PAD], [UNK]) without specific meanings?. 

We did not specifically assume it, but if the PAD token is used, it will be ignored by the models. We want to keep the positional information of inputs to avoid excessive information loss. In addition, we conduct experiments with RSMI-NoMask as shown in Table 2. RSMI-NoMask is a model trained without the masking process. The point of the masking process is to denoise adversarial perturbations.   

### The proposed method can be regarded as an MLM-like objective. A more fair baseline for comparison is using random masking, e.g., masking salient tokens with random tokens instead of perturbations generated by an attack algorithm.

We already conducted studies for comparing gradient-guided masking and random masking strategy and summarized the results in Table 6. In sum, our gradient-guided masking is more effective than the random masking strategy. 


### It is not clear how the framework improves robustness. It is pleased that the proposed method achieves non-trivial results on RAcc and ASR. The source of gain is still not clear. For example, what is the divergence of the output embeddings of the encoder? And what about the attention matrix is like?

We investigated embedding space changes in Appendix C and conducted extensive empirical and theoretical studies. With regard to the embedding, we compare the L2 distance and cosine similarity distance to observe the robustness of RSMI. The plots of Fig. 2. show that RSMI tends to show low L2 distances and high cosine similarities between embeddings of clean samples and that of adversarial examples. 

### The common point of RSMI and text attack (e.g., TextFooler, BAE) are that they both pick out the Top-K important tokens and replace them. It may help if the author demonstrates which tokens in the sentence are more likely to be chosen guided by the gradient.

It is hard to compare since RSMI computes gradients and masks tokens whenever it gets inputs under attacks. As shown in Table 2, there are typically hundreds of queries with randomness due to the stochastic nature of RSMI. Instead, we refer GradMask [1] which showed the effectiveness of gradient signals for detecting adversarial perturbations in adversarial examples. 

[1] Han Cheol Moon, Shafiq Joty, and Xu Chi. 2022. GradMask: Gradient-Guided Token Masking for Textual Adversarial Example Detection. In Proceedings of the 28th ACM SIGKDD Conference on Knowledge Discovery and Data Mining (KDD '22). Association for Computing Machinery, New York, NY, USA, 3603–3613. https://doi.org/10.1145/3534678.3539206

content.summary_of_the_paper:
This paper presents a new defense against adversarial examples for text classifiers based on pretrained language models. There are three main ideas used in this paper --- (1) random insertion of noise in the hidden layers of the classifier, which provides provably robust guarantees [1]; (2) masking of salient words during training, to encourage the model to rely on a variety of features while classifying text; (3) a sampling-based majority vote procedure during inference which preserves accuracy but confuses the adversarial attacks while they attempt to find perturbation directions.

The paper performs several experiments and ablation studies to confirm the efficacy of their defense, which outperforms several competitive baselines against a variety of attacks.

[1] - https://arxiv.org/abs/1902.02918
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
**Strengths**

1. An interesting set of ideas for defending textual classifiers which are intuitive and well-grounded in prior work.

2. A good experimental setup testing the robustness of this defense on 3 datasets, 4 models and against 3 attacks. Strong performance compared to several prior defenses.

3. Several analysis experiments, including ablations of individual components, run-time analysis and effect hyperparameters.

**Weaknesses**

I have two main concerns with the current work ---

1. I'm wondering if the proposed algorithm would work against attacks which don't just modify words, but also bring about syntactic changes to the sentence? This could be attacks using syntactic paraphrasers [1] or style transfer [2]? The proposed method (especially idea #2) sort of assumes that the attacks are going to be word substitution attacks (like BAE / TextFooler).

2. The models used in this paper (BERT, RoBERTa) are from 2018-2019, and the field of NLP has advanced significantly since then. The paper would be stronger if similar results are shown on larger transformers, such as the T5 or DeBERTa or some of the few-shot models like OPT / GPT3. These do much better than BERT / RoBERTa on SuperGLUE, and I am guessing they are much more robust to adversarial examples given their strong few-shot performance.

3. Finally, this paper would be stronger with experiments on other natural language processing tasks besides text classification. Perhaps something like text generation, using attacks like [4] or attacks on machine translation systems [5].

[1] - https://arxiv.org/abs/1804.06059  
[2] - https://arxiv.org/abs/2110.07139  
[3] - https://super.gluebenchmark.com/leaderboard  
[4] - https://arxiv.org/abs/1908.07125  
[5] - https://aclanthology.org/2021.acl-long.153
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
*Clarity* - Pretty good. The mathematical notation is a bit dense, but understandable after 2 passes through the text.

*Quality* - Very thorough experiments overall. I would have liked other models / tasks being tested (weakness #2, #3), but the experiments on the current set of tasks / models look solid to me.

*Novelty* - Moderate. I think many of the individual ideas have appeared in some form in previous works (randomized smoothing in [1], the gradient based masking is a direct inverse of attacks like TextFooler [2], the majority voting strategy reminded me a bit of MixMatch [3]). Nevertheless, I've not seen this combination of ideas being applied together in this form, and I think that is ok for novelty.

*Reproducibility* - Should be fully reproducible.

[1] - https://arxiv.org/abs/1902.02918  
[2] - https://arxiv.org/pdf/1907.11932.pdf  
[3] - https://arxiv.org/abs/1905.02249
content.summary_of_the_review: I thought the ideas were interesting (but moderately novel) and the experimental setup was solid. However, weakness #2 and #3 are concerns for me and make this work less relevant to modern NLP research, since the field is moving away from smaller models (< 500M parameters) and away from classification tasks given the strong performance of current transformers. I am currently leaning reject, but can consider raising the score if the authors have a strong rebuttal / justification for my weakness #2/#3.

content.title: Response to Reviewer TskH
content.comment:
### I'm wondering if the proposed algorithm would work against attacks which don't just modify words, but also bring about syntactic changes to the sentence? This could be attacks using syntactic paraphrasers [1] or style transfer [2]? The proposed method (especially idea #2) sort of assumes that the attacks are going to be word substitution attacks (like BAE / TextFooler).

While syntactic paraphrasing level study could also be an interesting research direction, we focused on word-level attacks in this work since they can be considered as the standard robustness benchmarking attack algorithms. Also, the quality and the efficiency of the word-level adversarial examples are significantly better than SCPN and we also observed significant degradations of the semantics of the original inputs especially when we apply it to long sequences like IMDb reviews. Moreover, most defense algorithms typically fail to protect NLP systems effectively against the word-level attacks. Thus, we focused on the word-level attacks

### The models used in this paper (BERT, RoBERTa) are from 2018-2019, and the field of NLP has advanced significantly since then. The paper would be stronger if similar results are shown on larger transformers, such as the T5 or DeBERTa or some of the few-shot models like OPT / GPT3. These do much better than BERT / RoBERTa on SuperGLUE, and I am guessing they are much more robust to adversarial examples given their strong few-shot performance.

There have indeed been significant advances in NLP, but we believe that BERT and RoBERTa are enough to show our claims for several reasons: First, it is true that overall model robustness tends to increase as we increase the number of model size and this tendency can be even considered as a universal phenomenon [1]. We also observed this phenomenon in our large-scale model experiments. Thus, it might be trivial to expect overall robustness improvements with the advanced models. Second, many advances in NLP including T5 and DeBERTa you mentioned are based on Transformer architectures and share many similarities with BERT and RoBERTa models. In this work, we focused on validating the effectiveness and the efficiency of RSMI through large-scale studies with fairness and theoretical studies.

[1] Bubeck, Sébastien, and Mark Sellke. "A universal law of robustness via isoperimetry." Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 34 (2021): 28811-28822.

### Finally, this paper would be stronger with experiments on other natural language processing tasks besides text classification. Perhaps something like text generation, using attacks like [4] or attacks on machine translation systems [5].

Thank you for your valuable input. Although we mainly focused on text classification tasks, it would be interesting to conduct experiments with other tasks. In the case of machine translation (MT) tasks, we first admit that RSMI approach would be too aggressive due to the masking process of RSMI. However, RSMI-NoMask would provide strong robustness by exploiting the robustness bound forming property of the randomized smoothing. 

Also, after reading the MT model attack paper you mentioned, we found that the WSLS attack algorithm is similar to BAE in that it uses MLM models for evaluating word saliency and perturbing input sentences at the word-level. As shown in our experiment results, RSMI defends the systems effectively against BAE. Thus, we strongly believe that our algorithm can efficiently defend the WSLS algorithm.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
This paper introduces two techniques to improve the adversarial robustness of NLP systems.

The first is to leverage randomized smoothing in each layer, with the theoretical guarantee of the perturbed model in Theorem 1.

The second is to mask certain tokens according to their gradient norms, to serve as a denoising process for reducing the strength of an attack.

Experiments on 3  datasets in two tasks are used to demonstrate the adversarial robustness of the proposed methods on some generated adversarial examples from the original test set.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths
-The proposed two techniques are reasonable and the results are good.


Weakness
My main concern is that the authors assume that the model has a continuous input space R^d, and they use this assumption in deriving all their following results. They argue that this can be cast with the input of text data as with their word embedding. However, they later consider the embedding layer as a layer and also inject noise into this layer. This seems contradictory to me.  If the word embedding is not treated as input but as a layer, I wonder if the theoretical results still hold.

The replacement of a salient token with a mask token is not clearly justified. Since the mask token is still a token in the vocabulary and it would have its gradient during the optimization of the BERT-based model, this replacement operation should then equal to replace the embedding of x_t to the embedding of [MASK]. From this understanding, the derivation of (4) may also be problematic.

I also have a small question about the results of RSMI-NoMask. It cannot outperform SAFER on QNLI (RACC on BERT-base and AvgQ on both models with the attack methods TF and PWWS in Table 2). There is no analysis of such results and could you provide some explanation why the proposed RSMI does not perform well under these cases? Also, I think a detailed discussion on the compared adversarial robustness method over different generated attack samples are needed. Moreover, the compared method and the adversarial sample generation should be described more, at least in the appendix.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: Actually, the  "discrete" nature of text can be addressed by regarding each token as a gumbel softmax distribution of the indices. For example, the reference "Gradient-based Adversarial Attacks against Text Transformers" and a few others. The authors seemingly do not know such techniques and can only sidestep this problem by treating the input with the continuous input embedding space, which is not a satisfying solution to me.
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall, the authors claim that they can address the issue of adversarial robustness of large-scale deep NLP systems, which have a "discrete" nature of its data. However, they try to sidestep this problem and use a formulation with a continuous input space to develop their methods. Both the theoretical and experimental results are a bit unclear, and may be problematic.

content.title: Response to Reviewer ZSMc.
content.comment:
### My main concern is that the authors assume that the model has a continuous input space R^d, and they use this assumption in deriving all their following results. They argue that this can be cast with the input of text data as with their word embedding. However, they later consider the embedding layer as a layer and also inject noise into this layer. This seems contradictory to me. If the word embedding is not treated as input but as a layer, I wonder if the theoretical results still hold.

Word embeddings can be extracted from an embedding layer. We just consider the word embeddings as an input to be perturbed in a continuous space since randomized smoothing (RS) algorithms train models with perturbed inputs to form robust radii around input representations. Thus, we're unsure where the ambiguity lies.

### The replacement of a salient token with a mask token is not clearly justified. Since the mask token is still a token in the vocabulary and it would have its gradient during the optimization of the BERT-based model, this replacement operation should then equal to replace the embedding of x_t to the embedding of [MASK]. From this understanding, the derivation of (4) may also be problematic.

We present several reasons for justifying the masking process:
1) It works as a denoising process (c.f., Appendix A.6).
2) It is a regularization for forcing models to exploit surrounding contexts.
3) It has a close connection to synonym-based models as shown in our derivation in Eq. 4.

It seems you are pointing out the mask token embedding update part, but we are not sure what's the issue of our derivation to relate the masked inference to the synonym-based inference. Could you provide more details?

### I also have a small question about the results of RSMI-NoMask. It cannot outperform SAFER on QNLI (RAcc on BERT-base and AvgQ on both models with the attack methods TF and PWWS in Table 2). There is no analysis of such results and could you provide some explanation why the proposed RSMI does not perform well under these cases? Also, I think a detailed discussion on the compared adversarial robustness method over different generated attack samples are needed. Moreover, the compared method and the adversarial sample generation should be described more, at least in the appendix.

The analysis is in Appendix F. Our analysis reveals that SAFER has an attack obfuscation issue which can be easily broken by estimating an average attack direction. In this work, we insist that SAFER relies on the attack obfuscation rather than improving the robustness of systems. In sum, SAFER is not safe enough and there is a way to attack them effectively.

### Actually, the "discrete" nature of text can be addressed by regarding each token as a gumbel softmax distribution of the indices. For example, the reference "Gradient-based Adversarial Attacks against Text Transformers" and a few others. The authors seemingly do not know such techniques and can only sidestep this problem by treating the input with the continuous input embedding space, which is not a satisfying solution to me.

Thank you for your suggestion. However, as shown in our table, our method significantly outperforms the gradient-based works such as FreeLB and InfoBERT. With regard to the Gumbel softmax, it seems you are encouraging us to use it for computing gradients, but it would be hard to justify the use of Gumbel softmax since it is a biased estimation of the true gradient. Moreover, there is no clear evidence that Gumbel-based estimation outperforms the gradient-based approaches in terms of the robustness aspects. Also, randomized smoothing techniques have a clear advantage in that it provides certified robustness, which cannot be obtained by using empirical methods such as the gradient-based approaches. Could you elaborate more on your dissatisfaction with our method or provide any literature that shows the superiority of Gumbel softmax over our method?
